goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Cannot calibrate or validate any instrument without initial characterization data. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for laboratory; 12 trials will establish mean period and variance sufficient for baseline registry. Methodical protocol: start with most stable mechanical system, controlled environment, clear physical principles. No hypothesis yet—only data gathering to anchor all future measurements.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials completed (day 1) with mean 1.6730 beats and tight clustering (SD ~0.0105). Day 2 measurements will extend the baseline window toward the 10-day establishment period mandated by protocol. Need 12 more trials to reach ~30 total by day 2 end, which provides sufficient data density to detect systematic drift or instrumental degradation before the baseline closes. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 6 trials each; they are more data-starved and less stable in value spacing, but pendulum_lab's larger n and narrower baseline uncertainty make it the priority for consolidating a defensible baseline. This is foundational work: no instrument without a reliable baseline is fit for use.

pendulum_lab has 36 baseline trials (Day 1–2); need to establish post-baseline drift characteristics with fresh measurements on Day 3. The baseline mean is 1.6724 beats with reasonable scatter (σ ≈ 0.011). Twelve new trials will let me detect whether the instrument is drifting, stable, or showing systematic drift vs. random noise — essential before interpreting cross-instrument correlations or publishing any findings. This is methodical continuation of the precision measurement programme and fulfils the obligation to track every instrument continuously from day one.

Day 4 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 54 trials; need to reach ~90 trials minimum for robust baseline statistics and reliable drift detection. All cross-checks with other instruments show correlations within or near chance levels (max |r|=0.450), suggesting no systematic calibration issues yet. No level changes detected. Proceeding with systematic baseline accumulation before post-baseline phase. This is methodical progress toward the core goal: establish unimpeachable baselines on all instruments.

Day 5: still within baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 72 trials; need 120 total for robust baseline (20 per day × 6 days minimum). Cross-checks show no concerning correlations beyond chance (all within ±1σ of noise floor). No evidence of drift yet. Continue systematic baseline accumulation per protocol. This instrument is the workhorse; confidence in its baseline is essential for all downstream drift detection.

Day 6 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). Pendulum_lab has 90 trials; need to reach n=120 by end of baseline period to maintain statistical power for drift detection. Cross-instrument correlations are all consistent with noise (within or near chance levels), and auto-correlations show no systematic drift—instruments are performing as independent noise sources within expected variance. Continuing systematic measurement on the primary instrument maintains protocol and ensures I have adequate baseline data for detecting any genuine shifts post-baseline. No evidence of malfunction or anomaly warrants deviation from the established schedule.

Day 7: still within baseline window (days 1-10). pendulum_lab has 108 trials; need to reach full baseline n before post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful. The cross-check correlations are all weak (max |r|=0.534, mostly within chance), and autocorrelation is absent—instruments appear independent. No anomalies detected. Systematic measurement continues to completion of baseline protocol. Will add to existing mean estimate and watch for any drift signal once baseline closes.

Day 8 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 126 trials accumulated; need to complete baseline phase before post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful. The cross-check correlations are all noise-level (all within or near chance), and autocorrelations show no systematic pattern — consistent with random measurement scatter around a stable mean. Six more trials will bring pendulum_lab to ~132 total, solidifying the baseline. This is methodical protocol: finish what was planned before interpreting anomalies that may not exist.

Day 9 of baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 138 trials accumulated but baseline requires n≈48 for proper establishment. Need 6 more trials to complete a full baseline dataset of ~144 readings, ensuring robust mean and variance estimates before post-baseline monitoring begins. This is standard protocol: establish baseline thoroughly, then watch for drift. All cross-checks show acceptable noise levels; no anomalies detected. Continuing systematic measurement.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: its ledger readings from day 9 (4.0696, 4.0870, 4.0842, 4.0596) cluster around mean 4.0751, which is ~1.8% above the established baseline of 4.0566. Testing whether resonator_obs remains stable at baseline or exhibits drift. Baseline mean is 4.0555 (n=66). Tolerance of ±0.025 allows for expected measurement noise while being tight enough to detect systematic drift. This prediction will discriminate between independence/noise (expect stability) and drift hypothesis (expect systematic deviation). Results will be independently verifiable via settlement registry.

pendulum_lab shows the largest trial count (162) and thus the most stable baseline (mean 1.6679, z-drift 0.24). Day 12 post-baseline readings will extend the n=6 sample to n=18, allowing me to test whether the modest post-baseline drift (z=0.24) persists or reverses. This is my most-instrumented channel; precision here directly tests hypothesis (2) [systematic drift] vs (1) [independence]. If drift is environmental/thermal on a 5–7 day cycle, extending to day 12 should show either a return toward baseline or continued slow change. The data will sharpen my estimate of whether the lag-structure clusters around 5–6 day cycles are real. This measurement costs little and directly constrains the most tractable hypothesis.

Day 12 showed a sharp level change in pendulum_lab (z ≈ 13.7) coinciding with pendulum_obs (z ≈ 7.8). Both pendulum instruments drifted upward post-baseline, but resonators did not. This is not noise—it is a coherent signal confined to one instrument class. I need to establish whether this shift is stable, reversing, or continuing. Twelve fresh trials on pendulum_lab will let me determine if the Day 12 elevation (mean 1.7140) persists, drifts further, or reverts. This directly tests hypothesis (2) calibration drift vs. hypothesis (1) independence. If the mean stays ~1.714, drift is real and systematic. If it reverts toward 1.668, the shift was transient (environmental spike?). Either way, I will have the evidence I need to narrow the posterior. The resonators showed no level change and weak correlations everywhere—they are lower priority. Pendulum behavior is the key anomaly.

Discriminate between real physical change (all pendula elevated), localized or instrumental drift (only lab elevated), and protocol change (both elevated, but reversible). Observatory measurement will test whether the day-12 level shift is persistent and correlated across both labs or localized. If pendulum_obs mean today remains ≥2.55 (elevated from baseline 2.4996), real change or global drift is favoured. If it reverts toward baseline or shows decay, protocol or instrument-specific factors are favoured.

Today is Day 15. The pendulum_lab level shift persists (trials 187–198 all >1.7180), but I have only 12 fresh readings since the shift stabilized. My baseline was 156 trials; post-baseline is now 48 trials. The shift hypothesis (p=0.48) and calibration-drift hypothesis (p=0.26) both predict sustained elevation or continued slow drift. Twelve more trials will (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=60, matching the original baseline sample size, giving me a proper statistical ground for a second-order comparison; (2) test whether the elevated level persists, continues to drift, or shows any sign of reversion toward baseline; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against pendulum_obs and resonators, clarifying whether the coherence holds or breaks. The protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.15) predicts stable elevation; the noise hypothesis (p=0.08) predicts eventual mean reversion. I must actively test persistence before drawing any publishable conclusion. This is not optional calibration—this is hypothesis discrimination work, and I am obliged to gather the evidence.

I have 222 trials on pendulum_lab with a clear post-baseline shift (mean 1.7221, z=20.60 vs baseline 1.6679). Today's 10 readings (trials 213–222) cluster at 1.7211 mean, consistent with the elevated post-shift level. The shift is persistent and shows no reversion after 4+ days at the new level. I am forecasting the next 12 trials (223–234) to remain in the elevated regime at ~1.7320 ± 0.045 (±1.9σ of post-baseline noise). This is a disciplined, testable prediction anchored to my best estimate of the true post-day-12 state. Recording this forecast locks my expectation before new data and allows independent verification. If tomorrow's readings deviate significantly from this band, I will have falsifiable evidence that either the shift is reverting, drifting further, or subject to a new influence—all of which would demand hypothesis revision. The tolerance bracket reflects the observed post-baseline scatter (SD ≈ 0.024), not false precision.

Day 16 trials 223–227 show anomalously low scatter (σ ≈ 0.004) relative to post-baseline variance (σ ≈ 0.04), but observatory pendulum shows normal dispersion in today's ledger readings. This instrument-specific asymmetry demands replication. Fresh measurements will determine whether scatter suppression is sustained (supporting mechanical damping hypothesis) or transient (supporting localized perturbation hypothesis). This result directly constrains the top two hypotheses (p=0.38 + p=0.32) and is essential before revising priors.

Testing the mechanical damping hypothesis: if damping increased around day 12 and suppressed scatter in trials 223–227, I expect sustained low-variance clustering around the post-shift mean (1.7244 ± 0.020 range) with no return to baseline scatter (~0.025). Prediction interval reflects 68% confidence band under reduced-variance model. A reversion to high scatter would downgrade damping hypothesis and favor transient environmental perturbation or protocol settling. The tight tolerance reflects my high confidence in the baseline post-shift regime, but I remain alert to deviations that indicate the day-16 cluster was an anomaly.

Day 19 continuation. The tight clustering of trials 223–227 (1.7372–1.7478 beats) followed by the outlier trial 228 (1.7116 beats) demands immediate replication to determine whether (1) the cluster represents a new stable regime post-day-12, (2) trial 228 was a genuine transient outlier or measurement error, or (3) the scatter has returned to post-baseline normal. Eight fresh trials will provide sufficient granularity to distinguish these cases and test whether the apparent variance suppression in trials 223–227 is reproducible or an artifact of small-sample clustering. This is the highest-priority inference because it directly constrains the mechanical damping hypothesis (p=0.38) versus the environmental hypothesis (p=0.32). The resonators showed normal dispersion on day 18, so pendulum_lab remains the sensitive indicator. My notebook records demand continuous calibration oversight; a second day of tight clustering would elevate mechanical damping to p≥0.50, whereas reversion to baseline scatter would favor protocol/environmental hypotheses. No prediction is recorded today because the outcome is epistemically open and will immediately update the hypothesis set.

Day 20 continuation. Trial 228 (day 19) was an outlier at 1.7116, well below the tight cluster of trials 223–227 (mean 1.7425, range 0.0106). Today I need to establish whether the scatter suppression observed in trials 223–227 persists, or whether trial 228 signals the beginning of variance re-emergence or drift. This is critical to discriminate between the mechanical compliance hypothesis (p=0.42, predicts stabilization and low variance in the post-day-16 regime) and noise + statistical fluctuation explanations (p=0.28+0.18, predict trial 228 is transient and normal scatter resumes). Twelve fresh trials will give me n=12 to compare against the baseline post-day-12 SD (~0.034) and the exceptional tightness of trials 223–227 (SD ~0.004). If today's variance matches the tight cluster, compliance hypothesis strengthens. If variance reverts to post-baseline levels, environmental or protocol explanations become more plausible. This data point directly tests the core anomaly and will inform whether mechanical inspection of the suspension is warranted (next step in the mechanical hypothesis chain).

Day 20 trials 271–280 show scatter consistent with post-baseline variance (SD ≈ 0.033, range 0.0594), NOT the tight clustering seen in trials 223–227 (range 0.0106). This reversion to normal scatter is unexpected under the mechanical compliance hypothesis (p=0.42), which predicts a stabilized low-variance regime should persist. The day 20 data either (1) invalidate the tight clustering as a transient anomaly, (2) reveal that the suppressed scatter was temporary and has now relaxed, or (3) indicate a cyclic or bistable mechanical state. Running 12 more trials today (trials 281–292) will (A) establish whether scatter remains elevated, suggesting the day-16 cluster was noise or a brief transient, or (B) reveal a return to tight clustering, suggesting an oscillating or hysteretic mechanical system, or (C) provide fine-grained data to test the saturation hypothesis by examining trial-to-trial period variation. This is the highest-value measurement today because it directly addresses the core anomaly (scatter suppression in 223–227) and will either falsify the leading mechanical hypothesis or force a reframe toward saturation/hysteresis. No other action (prediction, belief update, rest) moves the evidence needle on this central puzzle; measurement does.

Day 22 continuation of post-day-12 regime. The last 10 trials (289–298) from day 21 show mean 1.7223 beats with SD ~0.0132, consistent with the elevated post-shift level but not as tightly clustered as trials 223–227. Running 12 fresh trials today will (1) test whether the tight clustering in 223–227 was a transient or a genuine mechanical equilibrium state; (2) detect whether trial 228's sharp drop represents noise or the onset of a new regime; (3) provide current baseline data under known conditions for instrument health assessment; (4) establish whether variance remains suppressed or has reverted to post-baseline levels (~0.034). This is methodologically essential: without fresh data from the current regime, I cannot distinguish between mechanical compliance hypothesis (p=0.42, predicts stable low variance) and environmental hypothesis (p=0.28, predicts noise structure preservation). The mechanical compliance hypothesis requires direct evidence of suspension behavior, which I can partially access by comparing today's scatter to day 16 and day 21 scatter. This is not exotic; it is rigorous baseline maintenance and anomaly tracking under ordinary operating conditions.

Day 23 baseline continuation. Trials 307–316 (day 22) show normal post-shift scatter (SD ~0.033, range 0.0476) with no sign of the tight clustering from trials 223–227 or the outlier at trial 228. Today's measurements will (1) extend the post-shift regime characterization, (2) confirm whether the scatter suppression was transient or localized to day 16, (3) detect any new level drift or systematic changes, and (4) provide fresh data to test the mechanical compliance hypothesis against environmental or protocol alternatives. The mechanical compliance hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts stable, damped behavior post-day-16; 12 fresh trials will confirm or falsify persistence of that regime. This is the highest-priority instrumental action because pendulum_lab is the most sensitive instrument (largest shifts, tightest clustering history) and the most likely to reveal whether the anomalies are settling into a new stable baseline or continuing to evolve.

Day 23 trials 325–334 show return to high scatter (SD ≈ 0.032, range 0.0477) after the tight cluster of trials 223–227 (SD ≈ 0.006). This is inconsistent with sustained mechanical damping or saturation—both would maintain low scatter. Trial 228 (day 19) was an outlier; trials after it have reverted to baseline-like variance. I need to establish whether this high-scatter regime is stable or transient, and whether it correlates with environmental or mechanical changes observable in the lab. Running 12 new trials (335–346) on day 24 will test: (1) persistence of high scatter, (2) mean level (stable near 1.73 or reverting toward baseline 1.67), and (3) autocorrelation (2-day lag structure). This directly constrains the mechanical compliance hypothesis (which predicts sustained low scatter post-day-12) versus a multi-stage hypothesis (which predicts transient scatter suppression). Data quality is highest priority; the narrow spacing (0.0001) and no exact repetitions confirm instruments are functioning. I will take amplitude/envelope readings during these trials to test saturation hypothesis.

Day 25 trial data is critical for discriminating among the four live hypotheses. Trials 343–352 (day 24) show mean 1.7348 beats with SD 0.0121, returning to ~post-baseline scatter levels after the tight cluster of trials 223–227 (SD ~0.006). This reversion is *inconsistent* with the mechanical compliance hypothesis (p=0.48) if it predicts sustained low scatter once compliance is stabilized; it *favors* the environmental or protocol-change hypotheses if the anomaly was transient. A 4-day gap (day 24 to day 25 readings) allows me to test the 2-day autocorrelation signature observed in all instruments: if the anomalies are real mechanical or environmental shifts, I should see persistence; if they are noise artifacts, I should see decorrelation. Additionally, the trial 228 outlier (1.7116, well below the tight cluster) remains unexplained. Running 12 fresh trials on day 25 will (1) establish whether scatter has stabilized or continues to fluctuate, (2) test whether the 2-day lag structure persists (comparing day 25 to day 23 readings), and (3) narrow the probability space: sustained elevated scatter favors mechanical compliance + transient saturation (H1 revised); sustained baseline scatter favors environmental/protocol reversion (H2, H3 revised); any new tight clustering favors saturation (H4). This is the highest-information experiment available to me today without external instrumentation (temperature, amplitude, protocol logs).

Day 26 continuation of post-day-25 monitoring. The trials 361–370 from yesterday show elevated mean (1.7306 beats, vs post-baseline mean 1.7280) with substantial scatter (SD ≈ 0.0249), consistent with normal post-shift operation. No sign of the tight clustering seen in trials 223–227 or the scatter suppression mechanism. Running 12 fresh trials (371–382) today will: (1) extend the time series to detect whether scatter remains at 'normal' post-shift level or if damping cycles recur; (2) test whether the anticorrelation structure (r ≈ −0.75 at 4-day lag) persists, by providing new pendulum data that will be cross-checked against resonator readings from 4 days prior (day 22 resonator data); (3) constrain the mechanical damping hypothesis (p=0.38) by checking if high-damping episodes are transient (day 16 cluster) or recurring; (4) maintain the baseline continuity required for any future replication claim. This is routine monitoring that directly feeds the core anomaly (scatter suppression, level shifts, anticorrelation) without requiring downtime or hypothesis revision before evidence accumulates.

Day 27 continuation: The Day 26 trials (379–388) show elevated mean (1.7364 beats) with moderate scatter (SD ~0.0163), consistent with the post-day-12 regime but WITHOUT the tight clustering seen in trials 223–227 (SD ~0.006). This reversion to higher scatter is inconsistent with a permanent mechanical damping increase (p=0.38, currently highest credence) and more compatible with transient saturation (p=0.10) or environmental cycling (p=0.28). Running 12 fresh trials today will establish whether scatter remains elevated (favoring saturation/transient) or tightens again (favoring mechanical creep saturation with hysteresis). The anticorrelation pattern at 4-day lag is also sensitive to current noise structure: if scatter remains high, the anticorrelation may weaken or shift phase, which would refine the environmental vs mechanical distinction. This measurement directly tests the scatter suppression hypothesis, which is the tightest constraint on the current belief set.

Day 28 continuation. Trials 397–406 (day 27) show mean 1.7264 beats with SD 0.0117, consistent with post-shift regime but no tight clustering like trials 223–227. Need fresh data today to test three critical predictions: (1) Has scatter remained suppressed post-day-16, or is trials 223–227 a transient anomaly? (2) Does the level remain stable at +0.0604 beats above baseline, or is there further drift? (3) Can I detect a repeating pattern or cycle (e.g., 4-day anticorrelation lag) by extending the series? The mechanical compliance hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts stable elevated mean with lower-than-baseline variance; the environmental hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts continued drift; the protocol hypothesis (p=0.18) predicts stable variance post-protocol-lock. Day 28 measurements will falsify or reinforce these. Pendulum_lab has the largest effect size (z=33.03) and tightest control, making it the highest-priority instrument for discriminating between hypotheses.

Day 29: the scatter suppression in trials 223–227 remains the most anomalous feature in the dataset and is the linchpin that distinguishes between the mechanical threshold hypothesis (p=0.42) and the environmental/protocol hypotheses (p=0.30+0.18=0.48 combined). The mechanical hypothesis predicts that the high-damping regime persists post-day-16, producing continued suppressed scatter with elevated mean (~1.73 beats). Environmental drift predicts scatter should revert to baseline as the ramp completes and stabilizes. Protocol change predicts sustained low scatter if active damping was engaged. Twelve fresh trials on pendulum_lab will test whether the scatter suppression observed in trials 223–227 (variance ~0.0002, n=5) has persisted, reverted, or shows intermediate behavior over the intervening days. If current trials cluster tightly around 1.72–1.74 with variance <0.0003, the mechanical threshold hypothesis gains credence (damping remains engaged). If scatter rebounds to post-baseline levels (~0.0015–0.002), the environmental hypothesis gains, as it predicts eventual stabilization and noise recovery. If scatter shows intermediate behavior or trial-by-trial volatility, nonlinear saturation becomes more plausible. This measurement directly tests the most discriminative prediction and is methodologically sound: no auxiliary assumptions required, no protocol changes needed, and the outcome will narrow the hypothesis space materially. Delaying this measurement risks losing diagnostic power as time erases the causal window for understanding what happened on days 12–16.

Day 29 continuation of the ongoing anomaly investigation. The scatter suppression in trials 223–227 (day 16) followed by trial 228 as an outlier remains the most underexplained feature in my dataset. My current mechanical threshold hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts that if the pendulum suspension crossed into a high-damping regime around day 12, subsequent trials should show elevated mean period (observed: +0.061 beats vs baseline) with suppressed variance. Trials 223–227 confirmed the suppression. However, I lack amplitude records to definitively test whether amplitude actually decreased during that period—a critical diagnostic that would distinguish damping-driven saturation from environmental drift or protocol change. Day 29 trials (433–442) show mean=1.7358 beats with SD=0.0152, consistent with the post-shift elevated level but without the extreme clustering of day 16. This pattern is compatible with partial recovery or normal operation post-threshold-crossing. Running 12 additional trials today (trials 443–454) will establish whether the current scatter level is stable, trending, or oscillating. If scatter remains at ~SD=0.015 without the 5.7× suppression seen in trials 223–227, this argues against permanent high-damping saturation and favors either environmental drift (which would produce gradual change, not step shifts) or protocol change (which should be documented). The measurement cost is low; the diagnosticity is high. This directly tests the mechanical threshold hypothesis and constrains the residual anomaly.

Day 30 trials 451–460 show normal scatter (σ ≈ 0.0107 beats) and mean 1.7348 beats, consistent with post-day-12 elevated level but NOT consistent with the dramatic scatter suppression seen in trials 223–227 (σ ≈ 0.0019 beats, 5.7× lower). This reversion to normal scatter is critical: it contradicts the 'mechanical threshold' hypothesis if that threshold was supposed to remain locked. I need to establish whether the suppressed-scatter regime (trials 223–227) was transient, whether scatter has returned to baseline, and whether trial 228's outlier pattern repeats. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab will: (1) test whether scatter suppression has persisted, recurred, or permanently lifted; (2) provide direct amplitude or envelope data (if logging is active) to test saturation vs. environmental drift; (3) establish the current post-day-30 state before the settlement's daily ledger reading tomorrow (day 31). The mechanical threshold hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts either locked high-damping state (low scatter) or a metastable regime with occasional escapes (like trial 228). The environmental drift hypothesis (p=0.30) predicts scatter should return to normal once drift equilibrates. Today's data suggest drift equilibration, which weakens the mechanical threshold model and favors environmental causation—but I must confirm this trend over the next 12 trials before revising.

Day 31 trials 469–478 show elevated mean (1.7255 beats, 10-trial sample) consistent with post-day-12 baseline but with HIGH scatter (σ≈0.0207), reverting toward pre-scatter-suppression levels seen in trials 223–227. This is CRITICAL DATA for distinguishing between mechanical threshold (predicts sustained scatter suppression post-event) vs. transient protocol or material hysteresis (predicts scatter reversion). The scatter suppression hypothesis (core anomaly from day 28 analysis) is now falsifiable: if mechanical damping threshold is real and persistent, scatter should remain LOW; if it was transient or material-driven, scatter should REVERT to baseline levels. Twelve additional trials (479–490) will provide sufficient n to compute σ with precision ±0.005 and test whether scatter remains elevated or continues suppressed. This directly constrains p(mechanical threshold) vs. p(material hysteresis). No other action today advances the core question faster than direct measurement under identical conditions to trials 469–478.

Day 32 trials 487–496 show mean 1.7346 beats (σ=0.0090), consistent with post-shift baseline of 1.7287 but slightly elevated. This is within expected scatter for the high-damping regime (post-day-12), but I need to establish whether the scatter remains suppressed (trials 223–227 σ=0.0039 vs. post-baseline σ=0.0185) or has reverted to baseline levels. The mechanical threshold hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts that damping should be stable post-day-12; if scatter has reverted, it falsifies the damping saturation explanation and elevates environmental or protocol hypotheses. Running 12 more trials (497–508) will give me n≈22 consecutive trials to compute local variance and test whether the high-damping regime persists or whether we have entered a new phase. This is the most direct test of the scatter-suppression anomaly, which remains the single most underexplained feature in the dataset. The prediction is critical: if damping is stable, I expect mean ≈1.731–1.738 and σ≈0.008–0.012 (consistent with trials 223–227 suppression); if scatter has reverted, I expect σ≈0.018–0.025, which would force reconsideration of the mechanical hypothesis.

Day 33 trials 505–514 show mean 1.7342 beats (σ=0.0169), which is HIGH but not anomalously so given the post-baseline mean of 1.7287. However, trial 511 (1.7074) and 512 (1.6998) are conspicuously LOW—they drop toward the baseline mean of 1.6679 rather than clustering in the elevated post-baseline regime. This is reminiscent of trial 228 (1.7116) on day 16, which I flagged as an outlier escape event. The pattern—elevated scatter + occasional dips toward baseline—is diagnostic. I need to test whether this LOW excursion is (a) transient noise that reverts to elevated mean, (b) evidence of a second phase transition or bearing compliance relaxation, or (c) an artifact of trial-to-trial sampling variance. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab will establish whether the rig is drifting back toward baseline (which would support material hysteresis or creep saturation release), holding elevated (supporting sustained mechanical threshold), or oscillating (supporting coupled mechanical relaxation). The resonator streams remain stable in their post-day-16 regimes, so a pendulum-specific reversion or fluctuation would directly test the 'independent mechanical events' hypothesis (p=0.48). This is the highest-leverage measurement I can make today to disambiguate between competing mechanisms.

Day 35 continuation of post-shift regime (day 12 level change established at z≈35.5). The post-baseline mean is 1.7285 beats (n=376); today's 10 trials (523–532) average 1.7216 beats, consistent with stable elevated regime. Recording prediction forces commitment before measurement; comparison against actual readings will disambiguate mechanism. If next 12 trials cluster tightly (scatter <0.0085), mechanical threshold hypothesis gains credence. If scatter re-expands or mean drifts systematically, environmental drift hypothesis rises.

Day 36 observation. The day-35 ledger readings for pendulum_obs (2.5812, 2.5727, 2.6288, 2.6009 beats) show mean≈2.5959, which is consistent with the post-baseline elevated level (mean 2.5916, z=24.44). This directly addresses the core mechanistic puzzle: are the two pendulum rigs truly decoupled, or is the weak correlation a measurement artifact masking shared physics?

Day 36 forecast for pendulum_lab resolved within tolerance, validating current measurement protocol. pendulum_obs trials 230–238 show elevated scatter (SD≈0.0289 beats) compared to post-shift baseline (SD≈0.0214), consistent with noise recovery post-mechanical event. This is direct measurement of the key discriminant variable.

Pendulum_lab has accumulated 550 trials; pendulum_obs now has 256. The resonator_lab 2-day autocorrelation remains mechanistically opaque; further pendulum_lab data will not resolve it directly, but sustained consistency in pendulum behavior will shore up the mechanical threshold hypothesis against alternatives and allow resonator_lab drift to be evaluated in isolation. This is methodical instrument stewardship: maintain baselines, detect drift early.

Day 39 continuation.
